title: Objects and the Reference Model

content.explanation: Objects are JavaScript's solution for storing complex and related information together. Unlike primitive values that store a single piece of information, objects can contain multiple properties and values. Examples include objects, arrays, and functions. Because objects can become large, JavaScript does not copy the entire object every time it is assigned to another variable. Instead, variables store a reference, which is essentially an address pointing to the object's location in memory. When an object is assigned to another variable, both variables point to the same object. This approach saves memory and improves performance because JavaScript avoids creating unnecessary copies. However, it also means that changes made through one variable can be seen through another variable if both reference the same object. Understanding references is essential because it explains many common JavaScript behaviors involving objects, arrays, and functions.
content.example: If user and admin both reference the same object, changing admin.name will also affect user.name because both variables point to the same object.
content.analogy: Instead of copying an entire house, you simply share its address. Anyone with the address reaches the same house.
content.keyTakeaway: Objects are copied by reference, not by duplicating their contents.

revisionSummary: Objects use shared references instead of value copies.

mcqs.question: What does a reference store?
options: A memory address to the object
mcqs.explanation: References point to the location where the object exists in memory.

mcqs.question: Why does JavaScript use references for objects?
mcqs.explanation: Copying large objects repeatedly would waste memory and reduce performance.
Both variables reference the same object.

mcqs.question: A company stores customer information in large objects. Why is reference storage beneficial?
mcqs.explanation: References avoid unnecessary duplication of large data structures.

mcqs.question: Assigning an object to another variable automatically creates a completely new object.
mcqs.explanation: JavaScript copies the reference, not the object itself.
